utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, would you have the next witness brought into the courtroom, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, you need your headset. Do you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what your name is, your given name, your date and place of birth, where you reside, your current profession, and your rank in the army, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Robert Alexander Stewart. I was a Lieutenant-Colonel in '92, '93, I was the British commander underneath the U.N. command in Bosnia, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll get back to that. I didn't hear -- could you give us the date and place of your birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say it. 7th of July, 1949, and I was born in Preston in Lancashire in the United Kingdom, and I am British.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please remain standing for a few more moments, the time it takes to take the oath, Colonel Stewart, according to the declaration that the usher is going to give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for having come to the International Criminal Tribunal. Thank you for having responded to its summons. This Tribunal, which is now hearing the Blaskic case, the trial initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor against the accused Tihomir Blaskic who is in this courtroom to your left. Colonel Robert --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see Mr. Blaskic. Where is Mr. Blaskic? Oh. Hello.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. You have seen him. We consider that it would be useful, in order to ascertain the truth in this case, to hear your point of view through several points that were mentioned in the summons which I assigned and which was submitted to you. First of all, the development of the military situation, that is, your point of view about that, you as the person at the head of BritBat in Central Bosnia in October and May, 1992 and 1993; the chain of command that you were able to take note of and to understand, you as a military man; the principal themes of the meetings in which you participated; everything that you observed about the character of the accused, what his reactions were to your approaches to him; and you could also give us your points of view as a military person about ethnic cleansing and the use of artillery, your point of view about population movements and visits to prisons. We would also like to hear your point of view about Ahmici, the causes and consequences, the investigations which may have been asked for, and any other information. You will make a free statement for the time that you consider appropriate. We thought that it would be about two or two and a half hours or even three hours or, if you want, an hour. You will decide depending upon the documents given to you. You can use your documents but you cannot present a prepared statement. For your information, Colonel Stewart, let me point out that this Tribunal has already heard Colonel Watters and Colonel Landry. After your testimony, the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Landry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel Landry was the Canadian commander in the European mission -- I think that's correct, Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you don't remember that, there is no point to speak about that again. Here you have more or less the scope of your testimony. The Prosecutor will ask you questions; the Defence will ask you questions. There will not be a cross-examination. But after the Defence asks its questions, the Judges will. You may now begin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. May I use a few notes, or do you want me to speak without any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can use your notes. What you cannot do is to read a prepared statement but, of course, you will need your notes and documents. These are events which are relatively distant in the past, so that you can use any notes that you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's good, because I do not have a prepared statement. So I will use my notes. In August 1992 -- to be precise, the 22nd of August, 1992 -- I was a Lieutenant-Colonel, the commander of the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire regiment. I was based in Fallingbostel in Germany. I had been in Fallingbostel for eight months, and prior to that, I had command of my battalion since April of 1991 and that included an operational tour in Northern Ireland. Am I going too fast or should I stop for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm told it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for thinking about the interpreters because this is one of our problems. For the time being, is there any problem with this rhythm? No. The interpreters are telling me that it's fine, and we thank you for paying attention to that. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 22nd of August, 1992, I was in Berlin, I was on holiday, and I was summoned to the telephone at lunchtime and told that the British Prime Minister had volunteered a battalion for service in the Balkans with the United Nations, which gave me a shock, especially when I was told I was the commander, because, of course, I knew nothing about the Balkans. However, I returned to my base, which took me, say, three or four hours by car, and this being a Friday, I think, I worked through the night with my officers to decide how we would tackle the problem. It was a hectic month that followed. We did not know what our mission would be. We did not know where we were going. We knew very little. So I trained my battalion for one month on basic infantry skills, particularly concentrating on shooting, medical, and the history of the Balkans as far as we could understand it, which is almost impossible, certainly for soldiers. I was summoned to the Ministry of Defence in London on the 20th of September, 1992. I was surprised to be summoned on a Sunday by civil servants. At 10.00 on Sunday, the 20th of September, I was briefed in historic room 29 in the middle of the Ministry of Defence by a series of Generals and high-ranking civil servants on the potential mission I would have in the Balkans. The problem was that there was no mission, and this is the first requirement of any military officer, as Mr. Blaskic will recall, and we didn't really know where we were going. We didn't even know what part of the Balkans we would operate in. But I was lucky, I suppose, because I was told that I would go with a reconnaissance party on Tuesday, two days later, to work out what the British plan would be. On that Tuesday, we flew to Zagreb, and in Zagreb, we arrived at the airport and went to a camp called Pleso camp, which was a United Nations camp but which also contained a British field hospital commanded by a British officer. It was at that camp that we determined that we would try to go to Tuzla in northern Bosnia because, to the best of my knowledge, the French had determined they would be deploying to Sarajevo, the Canadians had determined they were going to be based in Banja Luka, and the British were slow -- as they always are -- to make up their minds and get their bids in, so we didn't know where we were going to go, and so I was told, "Try and find a place for us, but a place where we will make a difference." It was my decision to try to make a difference in Tuzla, because Tuzla seemed to have been isolated by the war and no one had been there. So we thought maybe we would try and base ourselves in Tuzla, with an approach from Belgrade, and our logistics would come in from Belgrade. Thus we took two Land Rovers and we drove to Serbia. We drove along an autobahn, all the way down through Croatia and entered Serbia, driving from Zagreb. It was a strange motorway because there were no cars on it, only the occasional checkpoint. We got into Serbia and for the next three or four days we tried to reach Tuzla. This was difficult, to say the least. In fact, it was not possible, because every time we went near the lines we were either shelled or we were stopped. This was by Bosnian Serbs, Serb soldiers, or the Serbian army itself. We tried to approach Tuzla via the bridge at Zvornik. We lived in the field, and at one stage I did speak to a Serbian General, and I wanted to set up the British base in Northern Bosnia, and he thought that would be possible and, therefore, I determined that I would drive or get my way to Banja Luka and see if I could see the commander of the Bosnian Serbs, who we understood was based at Banja Luka. Therefore, taking one of the Land Rovers and an interpreter, I separated from the main party, which I think was two or three Land Rovers, and tried to go to Banja Luka, which was not easy. Anyway, we got to Banja Luka. Then I went to the main Serb headquarters in Banja Luka, Bosnian Serb army headquarters, and tried to speak to the commander there. I'm saying all this so that you understand, because on the 2nd of June, 1995, I made a very detailed statement to the court, in written evidence, but I did not include this information beforehand, because I'm coming to how I came to be in Central Bosnia because I think it's important. I got permission from the Bosnian Serb army to position my troops in their area, and I thought that was rather good. Then we would get through to Tuzla, one way or another, across the lines because the lines were difficult, but we would do it. After that, I returned to Zagreb, where I reported by radio -- I couldn't report by radio easily to London, because our high frequency radio was down most of the day because of the peculiarities of high frequency radio, but I was able to speak by satellite telephone to London. I was told that, actually, they changed their mind in London, that our requirement was no longer acceptable to go to Tuzla but that we would go into Central Bosnia. I have to say I was rather dismayed, dismayed that we had wasted our time so much, but that's not the point. The point is that Hercules aircraft arrived, and we packed our vehicles on them and flew to Split in Southern Croatia, landed at Split airport, stayed at the Internacional Hotel one night, I think, and then we drove into Bosnia via Croatia, approaching from the direction of Tomislavgrad. At Tomislavgrad we saw the first HVO headquarters and we went to see the commander there. The commander, I think his name was Siljeg, was not there, but his second in command, a Canadian, a Canadian Croat, was. He was kind, because he gave us a guide to take us into Central Bosnia, across the mountains. We would not have made it, I suspect, without a guide because the track was difficult. So we arrived in Central Bosnia. We found the United Nations High Commission for Refugees was present at the time in Vitez. In Vitez we found an empty school that was not being used by school children. It was empty. After some negotiations, we decided that this would make a suitable base for us. We made a plan which effectively was that we would position the British Battalion with one company at Gornji Vakuf, three companies in Vitez, with one of those companies earmarked to leapfrog forward to Tuzla when we could do that. The main headquarters would be at Vitez, which was my headquarters. That was the plan we made. We returned to Germany on the 30th of September, 1992, and on that visit, to the best of my knowledge, I did not meet Tihomir Blaskic, but no doubt he knew we were there. The second reconnaissance I carried out in Bosnia took place on Friday, the 16th of October. But between the 30th of September and the 16th of October, 1992, the cabinet office briefing room had endorsed the plan I had made. The cabinet office briefing room, Cobra it's called, is the operational, political directing staff underneath the Prime Minister. So the plan was set. Now I had to do what was normal for military officers, which was to carry out a standard reconnaissance with my officers. We flew to Split, as I said, on the 16th of October, 1992, and on Sunday, the 18th of October, we drove over the mountains, via Gornji Vakuf, where I left a Major, to Vitez. We based ourselves at the school. The school was close to Vitez. From there I carried out a reconnaissance. During that reconnaissance I did visit Tuzla by going over the mountains. The distance to Tuzla is something like 180 kilometres through the mountains, and I was determined that my 4th Company would be based in Tuzla by Christmas. That was my objective. The first time I met General Tihomir Blaskic was, to the best my ability, my memory, and using my diary, something like 0200 on the 21st of October, 1992. The circumstances were unhappy. Not unhappy personally between us, but unhappy because of what was happening. Almost while I was there on this reconnaissance, open warfare had broken out between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. This warfare was, as far as I could ascertain with my limited resources, because I didn't have many people with me, specifically around the area of Vitez going to Novi Travnik, that area. I had arranged to meet Colonel Blaskic, as he was then, although we never quite knew what rank Tihomir Blaskic was properly, because the HVO had yet to determine their command structure, as far as we could -- it was only during the tour that Tihomir Blaskic put on the rank, while I was there. I arranged to meet him at 0900 on the 20th of October, but he was not at the Hotel Vitez, which was his headquarters, because of the hostilities that had broken out. I met a man called Mario Cerkez, whom I understood was the commander of the Vitez area for the HVO. He told me that Colonel Blaskic was not there but was in Novi Travnik. I won't go into the details of actually what happened for the remainder of the day. Suffice it to say that I had decided that there was only one way that my own soldiers could be deployed, and that was if the hostilities had abated sufficiently so that we could get our United Nations troops into the area. Therefore, I would try my very best to arrange a cease-fire. The apparent centre of fighting, the cause of the fighting, seemed to be at Novi Travnik. Therefore, I went to Novi Travnik. A battle had developed there and was ongoing in Vitez too. There was certainly mortar fire, I could identify that, and possibly artillery fire as well. Now, my statement of the 2nd of June, 1995 starts at this point. I notice that it's 1.00, and I know that the court goes into recess. I have probably about 10 or 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to congratulate you for your military punctuality, and pursuant to what we ordinarily do, we will adjourn our work and we will resume at 2.30. The court stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Mr. Registrar, please have the accused brought in and also have the witness brought in. (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. All right, Colonel Stewart, we'll ask you to proceed now. Let us proceed with your testimony. I want to recall, for the attention of the public gallery, Colonel Stewart is a witness who is called by the Judges of the Trial Chamber. Colonel Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to extend the time that I may speak probably to about 40 minutes from this period simply because I feel that you are probably not aware of all the detail of the 2nd of June, 1995 statement I made, or it may not be exactly coming to mind, and it does fit in with what I wish to say. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Colonel Stewart. About how much time did you schedule for your initial comments before we ask you questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, and then now I want to have 40 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You yourself consider that you would take how much time? The free statement. An hour? An hour and a half? What was your original thought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that's just fine. We've used up about a half hour; isn't that right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is no objection. Take the 40 minutes that you need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I go back to the 20th of October, 1992. On the 20th of October, 1992, I was originally intending to meet Mr. Tihomir Blaskic in the Hotel Vitez at 9.00. He was not there, which was unsurprising because there was a lot of conflict in the area. Mr. Mario Cerkez was there. Mario Cerkez, who I assumed and I was informed, was the HVO commander of Vitez, through my interpreter, a British army captain called Nicholas Stansfield, told me that there was a serious problem in both Vitez and in Novi Travnik. The problem was that the Bosnian Muslims were fighting with the Bosnian Croats, and I was told that the Bosnian Muslim commander was at a school close by. A man called Zeljko, who was second in command to Mario Cerkez, offered to guide me to that school so I could speak to the Bosnian Muslim commander, the BiH commander. I did so in a vehicle, a Land Rover, and I met a man called Sefkija, I spell that, S-E-F-K-I-J-A, who was the BiH commander. He told me that he had instituted roadblocks simply to stop Bosnian Croats going to Novi Travnik where he said they were killing Bosnian Muslims. It seemed to me that I had no option but to try and stop the fighting because my operational orders were to move my troops into Central Bosnia without getting involved in the fighting, and if the roadblocks were instituted, there was no chance that I could get my soldiers into Central Bosnia; therefore, try and stop the fighting. At 2.30 on that day, I put together a task force of Land Rovers which I was going to lead into the town of Novi Travnik. Going into Novi Travnik was amusing because there was a lot of fire. I suspect the crossfire was not aimed at us but it was, as I say, amusing and frightening. I went straight, when I got into Novi Travnik, I asked people where the BiH headquarters was as I knew nothing about the place. I met a man called Lendo, L-E-N-D-O. He, I understood, held seven HVO or Bosnian Croats as prisoners, and I demanded that they be released instantly and that they would be given to me because this was not a war that should be being fought. Mr. Lendo laughed at me, but before I left him, a prisoner was produced, a man, who was very frightened. I took him with me, and I went in my Land Rovers across town, guided by this man, to a cafe called the Cafe Grand where I met Dario Kordic for the first time. In a darkened upstairs room of the bar, I met Kordic and several other HVO soldiers, and it was clear to me that Kordic had authority, the authority of the soldiers around the room. When he spoke, they shut up; when he spoke, they listened; and when he said something, they did it. On a mobile phone, we spoke to Zenica and to a man called Dzermo Merdan, M-E-R-D-A-N, because the HVO -- Kordic refused to deal with Lendo, who he said was a war criminal. The agreement was that I would go and fetch Merdan and I would bring Merdan to a meeting in Vitez. By the time I got back to my base at a school near Vitez, it was close on dark; in fact, it was quite dark. But I was required to go and pick Mr. Merdan up from Zenica. I took two Land Rovers and drove to Zenica and found Mr. Merdan in the town hall. I subsequently brought Mr. Merdan back to Vitez. At first we thought the meeting would take place at my base, which was at a school, but then it was changed to the Hotel Vitez. At about 2.00 on the 21st of October, 2.00 in the morning, I first met Tihomir Blaskic, to the best of my recollection. I think he was wearing civilian clothes, I cannot remember exactly, but I think that's the case. But it was clear that he was the commander, and subsequently I met with Mr. Blaskic many times. Socially, he came to dinner at my headquarters, and I went to dinner with him, specifically on Easter Monday, the 12th of April, 1993. I also met his wife, and personally I consider both him and his wife to be thoroughly decent in my personal relations with them. This cease-fire meeting that took place something like 2.00 to 4.00 in the morning on the 21st of October was a failure. It failed to stop the fighting between the HVO and the BiH, but I left an officer who subsequently, with the UNHCR, in the next week or so, managed to calm down the fighting so that my force could be brought back into -- or could be brought into Central Bosnia. I had to return to Germany to give out orders and briefings, but I returned as quickly as I could, and I am delighted to say, when I returned, the fighting had ceased enough to get us in. I want to choose points in my statement of the 2nd of June, 1995, just to highlight them. On the 22nd of November, 1992, Tihomir Blaskic asked me to retrieve some dead HVO soldiers from the village of Turbe, where the Bosnian Muslim soldiers were in command. I went to Turbe, and I could not get the bodies, although, to the best of my knowledge, I think a Serb soldier was lying dead in a cart outside the headquarters, and I asked if I could take that body away as well. But that was refused. I returned, on the 22nd of November, to the HVO headquarters in Travnik. Mr. Blaskic was there plus Colonel Filipovic, I think Kordic, and General Prkacin -- I hope I've got that right -- P-R-K-A-C-I-N, who was on the joint HVO-BiH council, or that's what he said he was, and he had been in Turbe with me, and I recall that he said to Tihomir Blaskic that I tried my best to recover the bodies for them. My own personal belief is that I will recover any body I can to return it to its family, regardless of where it's come from or what it is. On the 12th of January, 1993, an incident occurred at Vares. Apparently, one of my patrols was stopped by a soldier on the road, and one of my patrols offered that soldier a lift. That soldier got into the vehicle and was lifted somewhere, apparently. This caused a problem because the commander, Emil, who was the HVO commander there, immediately lodged a serious complaint that we had helped the BiH. To be honest, I'm not quite sure what happened, but the effect was to stop bridge-building, which my engineers were doing to try to get us a decent road to Tuzla where one of my companies was located and where I was under a mission to try and get UNHCR supplies and any other supplies up to the people of Tuzla. We needed the bridges to work well so that we could carry heavier equipment or heavier stores. So this was a problem. My point of this is to say that I was referred to Tihomir Blaskic for decision by the commander, Emil, in Vares, and when Tihomir Blaskic made the decision, the bridge-building began again. We were allowed to continue. My escort driver, Lance Corporal, Wayne Edwards was killed on the 13th of January, 1993, shot in the head, through the hatch in his vehicle, near the town of Gornji Vakuf. Subsequently, I made a formal complaint to the two people I felt were the commanders most relevant. One was Mr. Merdan, who I've mentioned, and the other one was Mr. Blaskic, because I knew him but I also knew, by that time, that Gornji Vakuf was probably not quite in Tihomir Blaskic's operational area. It belonged to the Tomislavgrad Brigade under the commander called Siljeg. Nonetheless, because I was close to Blaskic, I actually made a formal complaint to him. My belief is that my escort driver was killed not on orders from the HVO or the BiH, but in Bosnia at the time, there was a lot of maverick shooting and it's possible, and I believe it's highly likely, that my escort driver was killed by a Bosnian Muslim soldier firing without orders. My point in this is to say that I actually did continue to think that Mr. Blaskic was the commander or at least could actually get into the command chain. There is some complication in the relationship as I saw it between Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic. On the 4th of February 1993, Dario Kordic wanted to see me. At the time and persistently he told me that his appointment was Deputy President of the HVO. I went to meet him at the PTT building in Busovaca. He was very agitated. It seemed to me that he was also the commander of Busovaca at the time. The problem was that Busovaca looked like it might have been cut off or cut through and, therefore, the route to Kiseljak for the HVO would have been isolated, and the BiH army were coming south from the region of Zenica and seemed to have some success. I was requested by Mr. Kordic to try and stop the fighting, particularly in the area of Katici and Merdani. Again, at this time I was firmly under the impression that the local commander of Busovaca was Kordic, local commander. On the 15th of April, 1993, I was walking in Travnik. I was trying to talk to the soldiers on the ground, of the HVO and the BiH, because there was so much tension and not a little shooting. It was at this point (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) got a radio message and asked me to go to Zenica. I was reluctant to go to Zenica because it was really not an area that I was particularly worried about, but the point was that a man called Totic, T-O-T-I-C, had been kidnapped. Some of his bodyguards had been killed, and Totic was an HVO brigade commander in Zenica. So I drove to Zenica, where I attended a meeting between one brigade commander of the HVO -- there were two brigade commanders of the HVO in Zenica. One, of course, had been kidnapped, Totic, and the other one, whose name I do not recall and I didn't even know it at the time, was present at the meeting. Tihomir Blaskic was not and neither was Cerkez or anyone else I knew from the Vitez area. The next day there was real fighting. Serious fighting broke out in the Lasva Valley. This caused me to shift my area of concentration from the Vitez area going towards Travnik and actually try and concentrate on trying to stop it. To this end, I went to the Hotel Vitez, I think around about 10.00, to try and speak to Tihomir Blaskic. I was informed there was no one in command present at the Hotel Vitez. Nobody was there. As I approached, I was shot at or -- well, I don't know whether it hit the vehicle, and there was a lot of shooting. There were also a number of dead bodies along the roadside. My escort driver counted, because we went from Vitez on to Zenica, about 35 houses that had been destroyed in the last 24 hours and, of course, a large number of bodies, including the bodies of a family near a cemetery. Before I got to the meeting I passed an HVO headquarters, and on the way there I'd seen groups of HVO soldiers, about five to six, normally along the roadside, but around ten past ten, around about that time according to my diary, I passed this building called the Swiss chalet, which is several hundred metres to the southeast of Ahmici. There were, say, ten soldiers outside this building. All of them were heavily armed, agitated, ready for battle. Clearly ready for battle as I would identify soldiers. There were some vehicles there too, including probably a sort of multi-barreled anti-aircraft type weapon system which could, of course, be used on the ground. They didn't like me passing by. So I was glad to keep going, because I was on my own with just a driver. I met (redacted) about half an hour later and said that I couldn't spare any more time to stay in Zenica because my place was back with my battalion. I did not see Mr. Blaskic on the 16th of April, that is a fact, although I tried to. A further fact is that on the 18th of April, Tihomir Blaskic telephoned me. I cannot recall whether he did it directly, but he certainly made an appeal. As I recall, he was agitated, which might mean that he did speak to me, through an interpreter. He appealed to me as a professional officer to move and assist in saving the Croats at a town called Cajdras, C-A-D-J-R-A-S (sic). He said, "I plead with you," or something like that, "to help by protecting these Bosnian Croats who are in severe danger." This was on the mountain road, the other side of the mountain, between the mountain and Zenica, the Croat community. I told him that he had no soldiers left because all my soldiers were operating on the ground and he said, "Please. You can do it," or something to that effect. As I say, I have respect for this man. If he asked me to do something, I'd try and do it. So I deployed my battalion headquarters vehicles, which had not been out of camp, to the job, and I stayed in camp and separated my headquarters and sent my battalion headquarters to protect these people. They spent one or two nights in Cajdras and effectively that helped reassure the people. On the 22nd of April, as is probably well documented by this court, I personally discovered what had happened in the village of Ahmici after I had been directed there by some soldiers in the hills to the north of Ahmici. The reason why I was in the hills north of Ahmici was because (redacted) had told me that he wanted me personally to try and stop the fighting, and I had told him that I personally had lots of things to do, but he had told me become that he wanted me to do it. So I did. In the hills above, to the north of Ahmici, as it was, I was told that a lot of babies and women had been killed in the village of Ahmici, to which I did not believe that would be possible. I remember responding that I did not believe that, it couldn't happen, and that I would go and investigate, and so I did. So I re-crossed the lines and drove to the village of Ahmici. I discovered that I was wrong. It was clear that massacres had occurred in the village of Ahmici. I was extremely shocked. It was also clear to me that the houses that were destroyed were Croat -- sorry, were Bosnian Muslim houses and all that remained were Bosnian Croat occupied. Indeed, I was challenged by a local unit of the HVO as to what right I had to be there. My response was that I'm an United Nations officer and I have every right to be there. In fact, I think it was more rude than that, because I was in shock. Of course, I went back that night and I spoke -- I sent a message to Tihomir Blaskic, demanding to know what had happened and an investigation was to start. On the 24th of April, two days later, I actually went to see Mr. Blaskic and demanded to know what was happening. I wanted to know who had done it, who had been arrested for this and what was happening. On the 4th of May, 1993, I challenged a Mr. Valenta who said, once again, that he was the vice-president of the HVO, who'd only recently moved into the area, to the best of my knowledge, but rather like Kordic said he was a vice-president to the HVO, and Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What date was that? Excuse me, I didn't catch that. I didn't get the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 4th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge. I'm taking these dates from my diary. Again, I challenged and said there was no response to my requirement to investigate who had carried out the massacre of Ahmici and in the Lasva Valley surrounding it. Nobody had been arrested for 18 days because the massacre occurred on the 16th of April. I suggested to both of them that those responsible for ordering the Ahmici massacre were guilty, in my view, of at least complicity in genocide, although I have to say I'm not a lawyer and I think complicity in genocide was a fairly accurate description. I think I saw Tihomir Blaskic once more before I left Bosnia but I can't be certain of that. I would like to end by giving my impression and opinion. I want to place on record that personally I have a great liking for Tihomir Blaskic. That was until the massacre of Ahmici. I considered him someone I could trust and who was good for his word and a professional officer, and I was disappointed in his response after the massacre in Ahmici. I knew that Mr. Blaskic was ex-Yugoslav national army and so was Mr. Merdan. They knew one another well. To start with, I always considered Tihomir Blaskic was the commander. Kordic was a complication. But I knew from my sources that the HVO didn't think of him as a soldier in the same way as they thought Tihomir Blaskic. After all, Kordic always told me he was the vice-president of the HVO, and his background, as I understood it, was as a journalist. In my opinion, Blaskic's area of responsibility stretched from the north of Gornji Vakuf to Travnik to Kiseljak and at least up to Vares. It did not include Mostar or Sarajevo. He certainly had a main headquarters at Hotel Vitez and I believe another headquarters in Kiseljak, but, of course, he had the right to operate throughout the area to any HVO headquarters. Commander Siljeg, with whom I negotiated for a period of about ten days from the death of my escort driver on the 13th of January, definitely was in command of Gornji Vakuf from the HVO point of view. Commander Siljeg was someone who I personally disliked intensely. As I have mentioned, at times, we, the British, were confused as to the exact command structure, particularly complicated by Kordic. But Blaskic was the main link to Petkovic, a chief of staff of the HVO, and I saw them a couple of times together. Not Kordic. I am positive that the HVO carried out the massacres, the major massacres, in the Lasva Valley in April 1993. I find it very difficult to believe that the HVO command in Vitez did not know or did not order the attack on the village of Ahmici which is only 3.5 kilometres from Hotel Vitez. I do not believe that any command structure doesn't know what's happening with its soldiers that short a distance away. In conclusion, despite my great personal liking for Tihomir Blaskic, I believe that Tihomir Blaskic alone was the HVO commander in Central Bosnia and thus held command responsibility for the actions of his soldiers. Even assuming Tihomir Blaskic neither knew or ordered any killing, why did he do nothing when I asked for something to be done? I consider that nothing effective was done while I was the British commander in Central Bosnia, and I stayed there until the 10th of May, 1993. To the best of my knowledge, no investigation was carried out, despite my requirement that a full investigation, including BiH representation, should be carried out into the massacres in the Lasva Valley. Regretfully, I repeat that it is my opinion that Tihomir Blaskic was the effective commander of the HVO in Central Bosnia. As such, he must be held responsible for the actions of HVO soldiers, even if I believe it is perfectly possible that he was not present in person when such crimes were committed. That is the end of my statement. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Stewart. As I told you, in order to organise our work properly, without any further ado, I suggest that you answer, for a certain amount of time, approximately an hour, even an hour and a half -- we will speak with Mr. Harmon -- but the Defence will have the same time as the Prosecution. First you will answer the Prosecutor's questions. Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed. In light of everything that Colonel Stewart, our witness, has said, in respect of the number of questions you have -- I'm not asking for a specific number right now. We'll see where we are as things proceed -- but about how much time do you think you're going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President, if I could just take five minutes and consult with my colleague, Mr. Harmon, I think we will have a better idea of how much we are going to ask. I just want a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please do that. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we will probably use half an hour, 40 minutes or so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. You and I have met before. Welcome to The Hague, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could, while we are asking some additional questions, could I have 29C first be given to the witness? That is the exhibit with the concentric circles on it that I think is known to all in the courtroom. If we could just give that to the colonel? If we could just pan back a little bit on that, please? We're interested in the area here, Mr. Usher, from Vitez to Zenica. Thank you. Yeah, that's good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a map. The concentric circles are the distances away from the Hotel Vitez. And, Colonel, I would like to direct your attention to the morning of the 16th. You noted for us that on the evening of the 15th and the morning of the 16th, you were in Zenica. Are you comfortable, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you were looking up at --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm wondering where this thing is being displayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the television camera on --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I'm so sorry. It's just I'm blind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, if you may, could you just -- from the morning of the 16th, could you tell us the road that you took? I know you mentioned the mountain road from Zenica to Vitez, but could you just take a pointer there and just tell the Judges exactly what road you took from Zenica to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Can you see that (indicating)?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's the start point, up through Cajdras, as I mentioned in my statement, up to the top of the hill, and then down into the Lasva Valley and then to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, approximately what time of the morning was that that you came from Zenica to Vitez? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Seven-thirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, during your drive from Zenica to Vitez, did you see any ABiH formations along the way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Did you say BiH?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about Armija, army of Bosnia-Herzegovina formations.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see those?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: On the outskirts of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: A roadblock. And the guys refused to let me through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get through?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than that, sir, did you see any large ABiH formations that appeared to be moving down from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, both you and the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: -- speak the same language, and I congratulate you for that. You both speak very quickly, like I do. But I would ask that you think about our interpreters. Otherwise, we're going to have to stop much earlier. Please be kind, think about them, and also think about me because I'm following as best I can on the transcript and listening to the interpretation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I'm sorry to the respective groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you and I have to take probably a little pause between the questions and answers to allow for the interpretation, and I'll try certainly to slow down.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kehoe, you're more guilty than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the fact that I have been accused of this before, I do believe that you are correct, Colonel, and I will plead so. Colonel, on that morning of the 16th, did you see large ABiH formations moving down, attacking formations moving down into the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that time, Colonel, the 15th or the 16th of April, did you see a growth of ABiH formations in the Lasva Valley getting ready for some type of attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I did not, but then I wasn't necessarily in that area. On the 15th, I was definitely in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, did you have, as your normal practice, your soldiers in various companies out on the terrain examining what was taking place in the Lasva Valley and throughout your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they report back to you at any point information concerning soldiers in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, Colonel, did they report back to you that they saw or did not see ABiH soldiers attacking in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think they did, but I think -- I had large reports of HVO in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, based on the information that you received from your soldiers in the field and based on what you yourself saw, who was doing the attacking on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It was clear to me that the HVO were attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the particular villages that were attacked, if you were to attack a village, Colonel, would it be prudent for the attacking commander to remove civilians from the village prior to such attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's a difficult question to answer, that, because I wouldn't attack a village where civilians were present because it's not acceptable, and therefore, trying to -- and in fairness, trying to remove civilians would give away the element of surprise. But, I mean, I have to say that I don't really like the question because I just don't understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Then we'll move on. Now, sir, you said to us that on the 22nd of April of 1993, you went to Ahmici and you discovered the massacre that took place there. Just tell us a little bit about what you saw there, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was relatively early in the morning when I was requested by (redacted) to personally -- and I say "personally" because I didn't want to do it -- go into the mountains above the Lasva Valley to try and stop the fighting, to separate people away, to separate the HVO and the BiH. I led a patrol of about -- well, one platoon, that's four armoured Warrior vehicles, and I also took a section of Scimitars, that's two light tanks, and as well as that, I took my own Warrior armoured fighting vehicle, and I went down the road to the crossroads where the mountain road joins the main Lasva Valley road, and I turned left through an HVO checkpoint, up the road into the mountains. And at the ridge -- I'll just check the name -- I can't read it. At the ridge, I turned right along a track that I had never been down before, and periodically, I stopped. At this point, there were most definitely large concentrations of BiH soldiers in the hills. I stopped at BiH soldiers, and on one or two occasions, I pleaded with them to stop the fighting, and on the second or the third occasion, I was told that they couldn't stop the fighting because it was reported that babies and women had been killed in the village of Ahmici. I already mentioned that I was shocked and didn't believe it, but I said to the soldiers I would personally go and check this. And so I did. I came another route down. Again, I just had to map read -- we map-read through. We came back into the Lasva Valley and then led down the Lasva Valley to the turn-off that led to Ahmici. I drove through the village of Ahmici, which is about a mile, actually. It's a linear village, or it was a linear village. I went to the end, and I dismounted my soldiers and I then dismounted myself. I walked slowly down the road with my soldiers fanning out, checking houses all the way down on both sides of the road. About a third of the way through the village, I think, some soldiers shouted for me. I went there and we discovered the first house where we could identify dead bodies. A man and a child, probably a teenage boy, were in the front entrance. At the back, even worse, it looked like the remains of several people. Clearly one adult, possibly two women, and several children. So what I had said, I did not believe was inaccurate. Of course, this was well-documented because by this stage we had a lot of press around us. After that, I went back and I think I sent a message to General Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic as he was then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to that piece of correspondence and the advice that you received, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to give the witness Prosecutor's 456/56 and Prosecutor's 456/57. If I could show both of these documents to the witness at the same time it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify things, Colonel, the 456/56 is your letter of the 22nd to the accused, and 456/57 is Blaskic's letter back to you. If you could take a quick look at those two. We'll just discuss them briefly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first letter, of course, is the letter that you have spoken about in your initial statement and just now, your letter to Blaskic. Then Blaskic's return letter to you, in paragraph 1, he notes that: "I am ready to send immediately the investigation commission to the village of Ahmici." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about this investigating commission, Colonel. Did you ever see an investigating commission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask for one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about what you asked for.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I wanted an urgent investigation into who was responsible, and I remember that I required Tihomir Blaskic to also include BiH representation on this, this commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular commission, did Blaskic ever seek your assistance in setting this commission up and did you refuse to give that assistance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you -- did he ever ask you for assistance in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, this letter asks me but I don't recall anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in a particular testimony of Blaskic, at page 19165, Blaskic notes: "In my letter, when I wrote it on the 23rd to Colonel Stewart, and in all subsequent discussions with representatives of the International Community, I sought assistance in carrying out the investigation." In your meetings with him, Colonel, did he seek your assistance in carrying out the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. I think my meetings with him were to demand that actually something was done, and nothing seemed to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to an exhibit, and this is an exhibit of your meeting that you talked about, and this is an excerpt from your diary, Colonel. If we could turn to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 742.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see that okay, Colonel, because we have an extra copy for you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We also have a couple for the booths as well, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a note from your diary, of the 24th of April, 1993. If I can just take one moment while the copies of this are distributed. I'm interested in the first two paragraphs of this excerpt, Colonel, concerning the events of the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just waiting for the French booth to get a copy of that. Okay. "Saturday, 24, April. The business of Ahmici is really big now and I decided to go see Santic, president of Vitez, and also Pero Skopljak, leader of the HDZ. I drove into town in my Warrior and I found them both in the basement of the PTT building. I was fairly to the point. I informed them about what I had seen in Ahmici, that it was a total disgrace, that it might have big impact on American opinion and put it to them that the Americans just might decide to arm the Muslims. In short, it was a disaster for HVO politics and those that were responsible should be identified and dealt with as soon as possible. In addition, I felt that the matter should be investigated fully with Bosniak Muslims on a commission that did so. After this I went to see Blaskic, who was in Hotel Vitez. He readily agreed that it was his zone of responsibility and that he must doing something positive. I told him that it needed action at the very highest level. For example, I suggested that the Security Council Ambassadors might visit Vitez later today. The impact would be severe and the HVO had better do something. "After that, I returned to the PINFO house where I briefed the press on what had taken place and in particular, Blaskic's agreement that it was in his area of responsibility. I stated that Blaskic had told me that the top level meetings were taking place about it too. In fairness to Blaskic, I also told them he seemed very shocked about it all!" Now, in this conversation, Colonel, that you had with Blaskic, to the best of your recollection what did he say about these troops that were in the area of Ahmici, if you can recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say they were his troops? Did they say they were not his troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I -- oh, yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, did he ever explain to you, when you were having these discussion was him about the events in Ahmici, that there was some dual chain of command and that he wasn't responsible for think soldiers that were in Ahmici? Did he ever say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I presume you're talking to me as "General."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I just promoted you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's very nice of you. Thank you. Unfortunately, the British didn't agree with you. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, he didn't explain any dual chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Although we had some suspicions there were some complications, as I've referred to earlier, there seemed to me, in apparent classic Communist style of approach, there could have been a political and military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to that, sir, with regard to the military chain of command, did he ever indicate to you there was some duality in the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you note in this particular document that: "In fairness to Blaskic, I also told them that he seemed very shocked about it all!"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I wouldn't have written that unless I felt it because, as I say, he's a decent man, to me. I was shocked and I he seemed shocked too, because both of us have families, and I always felt that about Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, let me show you a document that you probably haven't seen before. I want to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/58, which is a report written by the accused on the 24th of April, the day of your meeting, as references your meeting with Blaskic on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could take the document off the ELMO so the witness can read it first? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I would like the document to be put on the ELMO before you ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just waiting for the witness to read the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, in this particular document written by Blaskic, is there any expression of remorse or concern about the events in Ahmici? By him, not you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: From what I have read, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any request for an investigation at all in this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I cannot see any requests for an investigation, but I can assure you I made one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the particular statements that are in this document, Colonel, Blaskic says, at the bottom of the first page: "I think that Mate Boban should have been in Vitez today to indicate that the reporting is extremely biased." On the next page. If we could turn the page over, Mr. Usher. The second point down: "To talk about the extremely one-sided emphasis on the suffering of only one people, expressing the suspicion that journalists are being paid to report events untruthfully." What do you think about that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's laughable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I just don't believe -- I mean, if the press could have reported something -- the mainstream press opinion was that, actually, the Muslims were being battered at the time, and it would have been very good for a reporter to have reported something to the contrary of that. It would have got him better copy and more attention, but they didn't because that wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General -- let me ask you a question. I'm sorry about that immediate promotion that I just withdrew.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I like it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've noted there is no expression of remorse or concern about Ahmici in this document. When Blaskic expressed shock in this meeting, was he shocked about what happened in Ahmici, Colonel, or was he shocked that he got caught and that you are holding him accountable for it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. He seemed shocked. Whether it was an act or whether it wasn't, I don't know, but as my impression of Mr. Blaskic was as a decent man, I took it on face value that he was shocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, Colonel. In your experiences within the Balkans and in the Bosnia, had you had the experience that one side or another presented one face to the International Community and yet a different face among their own ethnic group? Have you had that experience, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The answer to that is yes. I wouldn't trust any of them. I didn't trust anything on face value. My judgment was that I would never believe anything either a Bosnian Muslim, a Bosnian Croat, or a Bosnian Serb told me until I saw evidence of that intention by actions on the ground. That was one of the lessons I learnt quite quickly, because I had spent so many days in negotiating cease-fires, and getting signed documents, and watching the deadline go by that I normally used to have a drink as the deadline went by and the fighting just carried on. So the answer to your question, in short, is that, frankly, I never really trusted what people said, but I did feel that Mr. Blaskic was upset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, let me turn to the next document, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 695, which is another except from your diary on the 4th of May, 1993, relating to your meeting with Blaskic and Valenta. Again, if you could just take a moment or so, Colonel to take a look at this. What I'm interested in is the last paragraph for the 4th, which is actually on the second page of that document, which starts with: "When lunch was over." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can read it quite briefly. If we can put it on the ELMO now. Colonel, if we can just briefly refer to this and just ask a few questions. "When lunch was over I took the ambassadors into Vitez and there met with Valentin [sic] and Blaskic. I stated that nothing had happened about a Commission of Inquiry into Ahmici for 18 days, that nobody was charged or arrested to my knowledge and that I knew the names of men accused - which I would give to the ECMM ambassadors. I insisted that the Government of Vitez was also involved in 'complicity in genocide.' By that I meant Valentin (who said he knew nothing about Ahmici until 2 days later), Blaskic and Skopljak. I said that I expected action and was backed up well by the ambassadors. After that I returned to Vitez Camp - having told about it to Sky News." Again, Colonel, you were asking about the commission of inquiry. Was this the same commission of inquiry you were asking about on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was, but I hadn't seen any evidence of any commission of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Blaskic again -- did he, at any point in this meeting, ask for your help to conduct this investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. Otherwise, I would have actually jumped on the idea and the ambassadors would have also backed me up. It's clear to me, you know, let's not beat around the bush, that nothing happened -- nothing had happened, and, you know, whatever way we put it, nothing had happened by that time and nothing that I saw convinced me that anyone was going to take action, and I saw the end of my tour in Bosnia as this happening and then it being forgotten about, but thank goodness, it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, another line in there says: "Valentin found out 2 days later." Do you see that little insert that you have there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day would that have been if Ahmici took place on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Colonel, that Valenta was telling you that he found out about it on the 18th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is what I would assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, the accused has informed this Court that he did not find out about this event in Ahmici until he received your letter on the 22nd of April, 1993. Given your prior testimony concerning the locality of Ahmici, what's your assessment of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I regret to say that that's a lie. That is my conclusion. I don't know it as fact. That is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, let me turn to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question contains something that our client had not said, namely, our client had said that he learned about the events in Ahmici on the 16th at 11.48. But as for the crime, as for the atrocities, he found out only later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, let me remind you, you will have all the time you need, after the Prosecutor has finished his questions, to ask your own questions. Let me remind you also that this is a Trial Chamber witness, and this is not the procedural scheme that you are used to, that is, an examination-in-chief and a cross-examination. You will have time to ask your questions. Have confidence in the Judges; you will have the same amount of time as the Prosecutor does. Mr. Kehoe, would you please proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I can move to the next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 743.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this note?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this in your hand, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is to (redacted), ECMM Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll just read it just briefly: "Ahmici Massacre - Possible People Responsible 1. Thomas Osorio (U.S.) and Payam Akhavan (Can.), both members of the U.N. Centre for Human Rights, have provided me with the following information: 2. Ahmici possibly had 800 (approx.) people in it as of 16 April 1993. One hundred and three were killed and --" What's that's next word there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: "Another."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- another approx. 35 are still unaccounted for. 2. The Government of Vitez is technically 'complicity in genocide.' That means Valentin, Blaskic, Skopljak, etc. 3. The following people were present at the Ahmici massacre: Santic Nenad Ivan Livancic Christo Zarko Vlado Krizanac - apparently said 'First kill the men, then the male children, then the rest. Destroy all that is 'Muslim.' 4. This information is provided so that you can use it in ECMM Ambassador's Report." This is information that you received, I take it, Colonel, from Mr. Osorio and Mr. Akhavan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that represent the sum total of people involved or were there possibly others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, many more were involved, but this -- my estimation was that it could be 40 to 70 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you noted for us that you left the theatre on approximately 11 May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I left on the 10th and I was out of Bosnia on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the time you left, Colonel, had you ever heard anything about Blaskic setting up any commission of inquiry?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, and neither did I give him these names. These names were given to me by the U.N. Centre for Human Rights. The advice I received was not to broadcast these names but keep them so that they would be recorded. I was desperate to actually record the fact that these names were known to me. I had no means of ensuring that would happen, and therefore, I used the ECMM to actually place it on record as I expected these ambassadors to actually make sure that follow-up action would ensue. That is why I sent that letter, simply so that a record would be made. My own government instructed me not to mention these names publicly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to move to another exhibit at this point, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 380, which is an interview with the accused by a Croatian weekly called Danas. Can I just see if that's the particular document? That is the article, Colonel, and I would like to direct your attention to the last question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, did you have the time to read this? I know that if it were your journal and your messages, things go faster, but do you need a little more time to become familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I haven't read it, and in 20 seconds, I could have a quick read of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We'll start counting the 20 seconds. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I have a few questions on this particular document. If Your Honour wants to take a break now and give the Colonel a little bit more time -- or else I'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that would be the best choice. Colonel, you're going to have much more than 20 seconds, you're going to have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please have the accused brought in, and be seated. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to direct your attention to this last question and answer that's on the ELMO, which is part of this article in an interview of the accused. The question is: "You investigated a crime in Ahmici. What is the result of the investigation so far?" By the way, this is dated in October of 1993, Colonel. "The investigation is still in progress. Information is being gathered. In any case, this is a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted once again to cast a blemish on units of the HVO before the world community. "After the crimes that Muslim forces committed in the areas around the Croatian villages of Lasva, Dusina, Gusti Grab, and other villages in the Busovaca municipality, the case of Ahmici was staged and skilfully shown to foreign reporters and EC observer missions with the assistance of the commander of a British Battalion at that time, Bob Stewart. "So far we are certain that the crime was committed by members of the HOS, Croatian Defence Force, in Zenica, which was mostly Muslim, and parts of the Muslim forces of the MOS, Muslim Defence Forces, and I've already said that the investigation is continuing. It is certain that the HVO does not stand behind the crime that others desire to attribute to us." Now, Colonel, this particular comment by the accused relates to you and the events that took place in Ahmici. What's your comment on this, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for being called "skilful" anyway. Of course it's absurd. The fact of the matter is that I was directed, truly, by soldiers of the BiH to the village of Ahmici, that is correct, but what I discovered there was a crime. Even when I was there I was challenged by HVO soldiers as to what right I had to be there. Now, as this was in the region of Ahmici, in the area of Ahmici, actually in Ahmici itself, and HVO soldiers were in the area, I would assume that they would be delighted if I was there if they had nothing to do with the crime. I make the assumption that I was challenged by people that in some way or other either knew or were implicated in that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Colonel, thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could you tell us about how much time was required for the Prosecutor to ask the witness his questions? Now, Colonel Stewart, as we told you, the Defence counsel for General Blaskic, Mr. Hayman, will ask you questions, and we will tell you about how much time was used.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor used about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Forty minutes? You'll have 40 minutes but it will be counted flexibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me say that before these witnesses came, the Court told the parties that with respect to the major witnesses, the most significant ones, the parties would have one and a half to two hours for their examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not getting interpretation. I'm sorry, I'm not getting interpretation. Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. I can feel that you're speaking vehemently. I would like to have the interpretation of what you are saying. Please say everything that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm speaking to the interpreters. I suppose it's been marked in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you hearing the translation now, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't know if I said two or two and half hours, Mr. Fourmy, but these are Trial Chamber witness, therefore, this is a Trial Chamber decision. But, in fact, we did set some time. I thought it could be rather balanced in respect of the Prosecution. I would like Mr. Fourmy to remind me of what was said, approximately. I've always tried, ever since we've had Trial Chamber witnesses -- let me remind you they are Trial Chamber witnesses who were not called by the parties up to this point. I would like to remind you of that as well. I simply wanted simply wanted to do something equitably. Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as regards the written decision by the Trial Chamber, unless I'm mistaken, it was said that the parties would each have one hour to ask questions of the witness called by the Trial Chamber. Having said this and in view of what appeared from the significance of certain of the witnesses called, each party was -- it was said that each party could have longer and that the amount of time indicated in the decision was the minimum, not the maximum, and that was the framework that each of the parties felt it could place itself. As you've just said the Prosecution used 40 minutes. This does not mean that a little bit more time could be given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But to go from that to two or two or a half hours doesn't seem quite appropriate. But having said this, nonetheless, Mr. Hayman -- go ahead. I feel you still wish to say something in respect of what Fourmy said. I don't want to take the floor from you, although we are using time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Since my earlier comments weren't translated for you, Mr. President, I would like to speak to you on this subject before you rule. At the Status Conference we had before these witnesses came, the Court said that as to the most important witnesses, the parties would have one and a half to two hours to examine them and that that was not dependent on what time the other party used, that they would have that. That would be a minimum. In light of this witness's testimony and in light of certain important documents that I have, and I have a three-volume set of U.N. documents which in part I need to review with this witness, it is not going to be possible for me to examine him in what I estimate to be less than two hours. I will do my best, but the fact that Prosecutor wants to try and limit me to 40 minutes so he spends his time showing articles which he claims were authored by the accused, although there's testimony to the contrary, that should not be a tactic that can be used to limit us to 40 minutes in light of your prior directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We agree. This is the first time at this Tribunal that the Trial Chamber is bringing in witnesses. This is a procedure which is outside the procedure that we're used to. Therefore, if you please allow the Trial Chamber to decide how it is going to have its own witnesses questioned, with full respect of the rights of the accused, whom we are not forgetting, and also to be sure that there is a more or less equitable distribution of time. That is why I asked Mr. Fourmy what could be done. I don't want us to be bound in advance about too much time, which might seem normal to you but which I -- I, who have experience for two years now in this trial, I know how much time could often be wasted by very detailed questioning which were frequently far removed from the purpose of what was being discussed. This witness is here now and I know that he knows that he has to come back tomorrow morning. I'd like to speak with my colleagues now. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: By calling its own witnesses, those who were not called by the parties, I remind you of that, the Trial Chamber has as its first concern the ascertainment of the truth. The Trial Chamber is not bound by any procedural systems to which you're used to and, therefore, it establishes a certain correlation between the Prosecution's time and the Defence's time only in order to ensure a certain possible proportion in the proceedings, and it considers that to be desirable. Mr. Hayman, let me reassure you, this is not because the Prosecutor only used 40 minutes that you are going to be given 40 minutes. I wanted to ask the registrar how much time could be used for you. After having spoken with my colleagues, we said that it would be reasonable to give you an hour and a half to question the witness and to ask him your questions. It goes almost without saying that after an hour and a half, we'll see where things stand. But once again, we're going to see where we are, not necessarily in respect of the interests of the Prosecution or the Defence but, rather, in respect of the Judges who must, in the end, make whatever ruling they consider necessary. Therefore, an hour and a half will be given to you. That is one hour now, and we will work for an hour, and you will have a half hour in the morning tomorrow. If anything is important that has to be further discussed, the Judges will decide, because as I said to you, it is not the cross-examination and the direct examination that are important, what is important for the Judges to have as much information as they can. Having said this, I think that I have protected the interests of your client as much as you have. It is now 4.30. You can begin. And I thank my colleagues for the wise advice they continue to give me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
