utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours, for your consideration of this matter. I have distributed Defence Exhibit 591. This is a new exhibit. It is in three volumes. There is an index to this exhibit. The index is at the beginning of Volume I, and Your Honours will see on the front page of the index, there is an index to the index. That's page 1, in outline form with Roman numerals, and the index to the index lists certain topics. This is at the beginning of Volume I of Exhibit D591. So if we're looking at a certain topic, we can go to that page of the index reflected on page 1. And then within the index, there is an index, topical-type index with tab numbers identified at the left and certain descriptions of the documents, the date of the document, the source of the document, and very importantly, whether the document is under seal. If "Yes" is in the "Under Seal" column in the index, that means that the document was provided pursuant to Rule 70 and must only be discussed in closed or private session. There is a mix in these volumes of documents that must remain under seal and documents that are public. I will be endeavouring to ask the witness to comment on some but obviously not all of these exhibits. Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, good afternoon, and welcome to The Hague belatedly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Belatedly? Why belatedly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, because you have been welcomed by others --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and I didn't have an opportunity until now to welcome you. My name is Russell Hayman, and together with Anto Nobilo, we have represented General Blaskic, myself since the summer of 1996 and Mr. Nobilo a couple of months thereafter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: And I've met you before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We met a couple of years ago in London for a couple of hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if you would remember. I certainly remember my pleasant meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: And I can remember my meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your contacts with the Prosecutor's Office. Have you had any contacts with their office since your written statement in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I have, in the same way as you interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had any contacts with them in the last three months?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. In fact, I was surprised, because I thought at least I would be given some direction apart from the Judges' requirement for me to be here. So the answer is clearly "No." So I am unguided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibits D341 and D343 could be retrieved?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. Harmon and I did meet with the witness sometime in March, I believe it was in March, and I believe that we informed Mr. Fourmy of that, and I believe it was brought to the Court's attention that we had done that. Thereafter, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I mentioned the issue of interruptions to Mr. Hayman. I would like you to get out of your favourite procedural scheme that you're used to. This is not the same scheme. If you have anything that you want to make clear, you can do that in your closing arguments. Mr. Hayman, please continue to ask your questions of the witness, as you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While those two exhibits are being pulled, Colonel, let me try and clarify something. You were called to a meeting in Zenica after the Totic kidnapping on the 15th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who called you and asked you to come to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: To the best of my memory,(redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to go. But I had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had a meeting on the 24th of April, 1993, with Colonel Blaskic. This is after the letter exchange on the 22nd and 23rd. Is it correct that (redacted) was not at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look in your diary and see if your diary indicates whether (redacted) was at the meeting on 24 April, 1993? I believe it's the first paragraph is the reference to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't see (redacted)'s name there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree, in your diary at least, there is no reference to (redacted) being there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a couple of pages later in your diary, on the 4th of May, 1993, at the top of the page, would you agree there is a reference to showing the ECMM ambassadors around and that: "When lunch was over, I took the ambassadors into Vitez and there met with Valentin and Blaskic." That's the first line of paragraph 4 on that page. Do you see that? This is the page above the 5th of May and the carry over from the 4th of May, starting on the prior page --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: You mean "When lunch was over," that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I took the ambassadors into Vitez and met with Valentin and Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was (redacted) with you on that occasion, 4 May, 1993, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I would assume he might be, but the fact of the matter is, if it's not in my diary, it is certainly probably forgotten from my brain at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then you have no recollection other than possibly this meeting on the 4th of May, 1993, prior to the 4th of May but after the Ahmici massacre, when you went to see Colonel Blaskic with (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. From the time period of the Ahmici massacre --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to the 4th of May, which is noted in your diary --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- do you recall any meeting where you took (redacted) with you to meet Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: In my memory, no. Maybe it is in the diary, but I'm not a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. It's been many years. If you see anything overnight that suggests there was a meeting that (redacted) had with Colonel Blaskic before the 4th of May, 1993, please bring it to the Court's attention. I would ask you to do that. If Defence Exhibit D341 could be provided to the witness, and perhaps the French could be put on the ELMO? You said that you were not aware of any order to investigate the Ahmici massacre before your departure from the theatre on or about the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have before you Defence Exhibit D341, which is an order dated the 10th of May, 1993, to conduct an investigation into events in the village of Ahmici from Colonel Blaskic. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. And I would note the time on that document is 5.00. By 5.00, I was almost in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were gone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the theatre, did you have any means of keeping abreast with what efforts Colonel Blaskic either was or was not making to investigate the massacre in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Not direct to Colonel Blaskic. Of course, I requested frequently from the British military as to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they brief you on Defence Exhibit 341?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now look at Defence Exhibit 343, a follow-up order dated 17 August, 1993, directing further investigation and setting a deadline in another 30 days' time. Is this an order you were briefed on, if you can say, by your government, after your departure from the theatre on or about 10 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's not, but I notice it's four months after the event. I mean, I demanded instant action and nothing happened, and by the time I left on the 10th of May, no action had been taken. In such instances, in a fast-moving situation, one would expect and require professional officers to take action quickly, and giving me documents at the time, you know, 5.00, after I have left and sort of four months later, I personally think that's way too late. It doesn't in any way exonerate the fact that action should have been taken immediately. It was not taken immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, if you could listen to my questions, it will facilitate this examination, and try and answer my questions? My question was: Were you briefed on Defence Exhibit 343 by your government or was it otherwise brought to your attention after your departure from the theatre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, my answer is "No."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to your entry into the theatre. Let me ask you first: Your diary, does it contain, the copy you have, the same date stamp numbers that mine do in the lower right-hand corner or only upper right-hand corner numbers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It contains neither. It is my own diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will give you dates and paragraphs to assist you to refer to your diary for sake of speed. Directing your attention to your diary, the entry for October 18, 1992, and specifically directing your attention to the beginning of the fourth paragraph, is it correct that as you travelled north from Tomislavgrad towards Vitez on the 18th of October, 1992, that about 5 kilometres south of Novi Travnik, you came upon a roadblock blocking the road, manned by the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could go two pages further in your diary to the entries for 20 October, 1992, and I would direct your attention to the third full paragraph. It's the fourth paragraph if you include the partial paragraph at the top of the page. On this date, you describe you went to Novi Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to the Cafe Grand and saw Mr. Kordic and some HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Blaskic there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you got back in the early morning hours of the next day and you saw Colonel Blaskic, that he was in civilian clothes and that you concluded he had been wearing civilian clothes because he probably had been trying to get into Novi Travnik dressed as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that was my conclusion at the time because it was not easy to get into Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a lot of fighting, a lot of checkpoints, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we came under fire, so I'm quite sure that anyone else would have come under similar fire, from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, after the fall of Jajce, the mutiny that occurred among the HVO soldiers from the Tomislavgrad area who had been manning the front at Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe it for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. This was an occasion when, to the best of my knowledge, there seemed to be a mutiny of HVO soldiers who seem to have come from the area of Tomislavgrad. They refused to soldier, what we call in the military "refuse to soldier." I had the greatest sympathy for Tihomir Blaskic because it seemed to me that he was trying to command an operational area with reinforcements from outside that area, yet these guys were withdrawing, and he had a serious problem and a problem that I am lucky to say has never happened to me. So I had sympathy for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these soldiers, although native to the Tomislavgrad area, they had been at the front against the Serbs in Jajce, is that right, as far as you understood?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Serbs, as far as I understood. Not necessarily in Jajce but in the village of Turbe and Travnik, and they were jointly defending that area, as I understood it, with the Bosnian Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a large group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah, it was. It seemed to be a large group of people because they spent, you know, at least a day or two sitting on tractors ready to go, and they were right the way through Vitez. It was an extremely embarrassing moment, I think, for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know ultimately, was Colonel Blaskic able to direct them as a military unit, or did they do what they wanted to do and did they leave the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say they departed the area, scuttled out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about the conflict in January of 1993, and I would direct your attention to the 25th of January, 1993. In the middle of the bottom paragraph on that page, it is written: "I visited ICRC and then went to the commander of the 3rd Corps, BiH army. I complained that they had really started this trouble." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The entry for the 25th of January begins on one page, there are three lines, then it carries over to the next page. At the bottom of that next page, in the middle of the paragraph there is a reference to your visiting who I assume was General Hadzihasanovic and complaining to him that the conflict in January really had been started by the BH army. Do you recall those events? If you need me to direct you to the actual event itself, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Direct me to the event itself, because I'm quite prepared to accept that there might have been -- that might have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of that same day there is a reference to an attack in Kacuni and the death of two HVO soldiers. That's at the third and fourth lines under that date.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third and fourth lines under the date 25 January.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when you spoke to General Hadzihasanovic and said, "You, the BH army, you started the conflict in January in Busovaca," were you referring to that ambush and killing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I probably was. You know, I was very -- I tried to be as even-handed as I could be and, certainly, let's get this clear, I was not in any way supporting any particular side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's a bit awkward, but when you answer my questions, please direct your answer to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Busovaca-Kiseljak road was cut or severed as a result of that January conflict, was Colonel Blaskic trapped in Kiseljak? If you need to refer to your book, on page 234 there is a reference on this subject.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't got my book. But it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. We'll move on. Now, in your diary, three pages further on, on the 1st of February there's a reference to visiting a warehouse about two kilometres off the road near Kacuni and finding in cells certain ICRC personnel, Claire, and Dennis, and Amela. They were interviewing about 30 Croats. "One, at least, was very old. The place was freezing cold and Clare complained about it. The detainees must have been really cold." Was this near Kacuni, off the road, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I know where it was. I'll look at a map. This is my operational map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the place known as the Silos, south of the road near Kacuni? Doing that help at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. It was a revolting place. But if you want to question me further, I can remember the place --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please take your time. Take a look.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere south of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 1st of February, 1993, there are 30 Croat prisoners -- by the way, were some of them civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: They were all that sort of -- they were old people and young people. It was a mixture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had they come from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Don't ask me. I don't know where they'd come from. I just knew they were there and I didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe they came from the area between Kacuni and Bilalovac that had been taken over by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. I didn't know where they'd come from. I'd just said that. But it's possible. It seemed logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's move forward in time to the middle of April 1993. There were some kidnappings of HVO officers and soldiers in the days before the 15th of April. Do you recall those kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Not offhand. Is it in my diary?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are various references. You recall no kidnappings of HVO officers prior to the Totic kidnapping on the 15th of April. Is that your best recollection now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is my best recollection now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention then to the 15th of April and to your diary entry. You went to a meeting in Zenica and the Totic kidnapping was discussed, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, it was the reason for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Because this was a serious incident.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It was a very serious incident, which I considered I had to go and attend simply because I was fully aware that if this kidnapping was not resolved, it seemed to me the whole of the Lasva Valley would erupt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 15th, did the BH army take the position in this meeting that the Totic kidnapping was not their problem and that the civil authorities were responsible for any investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is a position not far off the truth. I mean, I seem to remember that at this meeting that Merdan, and I questioned him and I told him to his face I thought it was appalling and that, you know, something had to be done, and I seem to remember him saying it was a matter for the chief of police or something, something like that. I can't remember exactly, but I remember being angry about it and saying I was very, very unhappy about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, and I'm reading from page 281 of your book: "This kidnap of a senior Croat officer in a Muslim stronghold created a terribly volatile atmosphere"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, there was another meeting the following day in Zenica regarding the Totic kidnapping; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the BH army took the same position, this was not their affair, or did they even show up to that meeting? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think Merdan was there but my diary will have noted that, and I'm not that au fait with my diary to know anything different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move forward, and if Volume II of Defence Exhibit 591 can be provided to the witness. I'd like you to turn to tab 89 of that exhibit. This is a milinfosum dated 15 April, 1993, and my interest lies in paragraph 2, "Vitez" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we have the exact reference, please? It's 89, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tab 89 in Volume 2, Defence Exhibit 591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I've got it. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Cheshire milinfosum dated 15 April 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I have it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which means it would have been drafted on the evening of the 15th of April, after certain events during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at paragraph 2, the Vitez paragraph, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving word, either on the night of the 15th or the morning of the 16th, that as a result of two missing BiH soldiers the BiH, that is the army of BiH in Vitez, on the night of the 15th, was threatening retaliatory action against the HVO unless the two officers were found?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. I remember another thing, I didn't read these. They may have gone to my staff, but I was very stressed at the time and customarily I would not necessarily read a milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would attend the evening briefing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Correct. I would attend the evening briefing if I was in location, which I normally was not, certainly at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'd like to go to a portion of tab 92, which is under seal. So we need a private session. We won't put it on the ELMO. I think Your Honours each have a copy. The Prosecutor has a copy. We don't need to go to closed session, we simply need a private session for a moment. May we do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Private session for a few moments. I'm saying this for the public gallery. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to an event that you described as follows, referencing a priest in the area. This is the bottom of page 288: "I told him what we had found at Cajdras and Podbrdze. It was obvious that almost a thousand Croats had been driven from their homes by the fighting." Did you, in fact, see that on or about the 19th of April, large groups of Croats who had been driven out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't only see it, they were blocking the road and they didn't want me to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, there's a picture in the Colonel's book. I'd like to put it on the ELMO and see if it comes out on the screen so the court can see this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we can enlarge the picture slightly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I apologise for leaning over your shoulder, but in the interests of time, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's you, isn't it, in the middle of the picture?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the rear.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: From the rear. What a lousy view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who are all these people standing around in front of your Warrior?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: These are Bosnian Croat civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they come to be there on or about the 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Some of them had been driven from their homes and they were at that village, Cajdras, and the man that was talking on their behalf was the most amazing man, who was a priest, who convinced me that I had to do something to protect these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that Father Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I just know that I had the deepest respect for the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there's already been testimony on that from the party you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it possible to take a picture of a picture, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Hayman speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They're raising their hands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The interpreter asked you to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpretation booth. I was asking the technical booth if it was possible to take a picture of this picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which means that if the usher wants to do his job probably, it's very difficult, Mr. Hayman, to speak that way. You have take charge of the book, which will allow Mr. Hayman to express himself more easily. Lower the light a little bit on the projector.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video booth said that yes, a photograph can be made but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hayman, the photograph will be made and we'll have a reference number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D593.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that day, Colonel Blaskic phoned you or spoke to you through an interpreter, I think you said you weren't sure, and pleaded with you to do what you could for the safety of these people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think he was sincere in that request, or was he trying to inflame passions and drive people out of their homes? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think he was sincere and I appreciated that, and therefore, I was determined to do something. I've already given evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you have. Thank you. Now I would like to direct your attention again back to your diary, and the date reference is 29 April. This is a reference to a visit by you and Generals Halilovic and Petkovic to a portion of the Kiseljak municipality for the purpose of trying to further implement the cease-fire agreement. Do you see in the middle of the second full paragraph that you describe a visit to a village called Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there troops from the BH army in Gomionica on the 29th of April, 1993, and did General Halilovic meet with them and speak with them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: My diary says it did, and as I wrote it at the time, I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those troops were about a mile northeast from the road up in the village of Gomionica; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to direct your attention two pages further on in your diary to the carry over entry for the 5th of May, 1993, and the specific reference is the first full paragraph regarding a visit to a BH army prison in Poculica that you made together with the International Committee for the Red Cross on 5 May, 1993. Have you found that entry towards the top of the page I'm referencing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Is it during the afternoon or is it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The end of the day because it grew dark, and that's the factual point I'll be asking you about. On that day, did you go, in the early evening, to Poculica and find that the BH army had interned about 20 Croat men, and was the purpose of your visit to try and secure their release together with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't like anyone imprisoned by any side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it take some wrangling and persuading to persuade the keeper of these prisoners to release them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ultimately were they convinced to release them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just read?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: "Yes" is the answer, and they did it because I asked them to do. Otherwise, I wouldn't have written it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a technical problem with securing their release on that day, the 5th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The technical problem was that it was too dangerous to take them out in night because we didn't want them to be hurt by people firing at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a condition that the ICRC quite reasonably imposed on the release of prisoners and detained persons, that release had to occur in a safe environment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the case on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: As I say, I can't remember. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it your idea that they should not be released or was it the ICRC's view that they could not do such a release at such a dangerous time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It seems, according to my diary, it was the ICRC, but I cannot remember from my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you agree your contemporaneous diary reflects that that was the ICRC's position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, directing your attention to the next page, there's a reference to meeting Mr. Valenta. That's on the 7th of May, 1993. I would direct your attention to line 4. You and Alastair Duncan went to see Anto Valenta, and is it correct that "I hadn't seen very much of this character before as I simply didn't know he existed. In fact, his office had been in Travnik until recently."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen him before in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was as of the 7th of May, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Correct. Could I just add something? This man, Valenta, sort of appeared like a joker to me. I had no knowledge of him before about this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have use --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: A joker coming out of the pack, I mean. Someone who has suddenly sprung up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please face the Judges when you answer, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know that it isn't easy, but try. Thank you very much. Mr. Hayman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the last page of your diary. On the 9th of May, you took Alastair Duncan and introduced him to Colonel Blaskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So my statement earlier was incorrect insofar as this is the last time I saw Tihomir Blaskic. I'm sorry for that, Your Honour. But my diary is right; my memory's wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conversation on that occasion? Was it a courtesy call or was there substantive conversation, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Alastair Duncan was with me. Prior to our meeting with Tihomir Blaskic, to the best of my memory, we decided that I would be hard, as I was leaving, and he would say little. I was particularly concerned that nothing had happened about the massacre of Ahmici and in the Lasva Valley, and I think that at this meeting I challenged Tihomir Blaskic on the matter of who was in command, who was responsible for the soldiers of the HVO, and I believe, to the best of my recollection, although it is not in my diary, when he confirmed that he was the commander, I believe that I said to him words to the effect that he will one day appear in court. That is what I think happened at that meeting, and I believe that Alastair Duncan was present when it happened. I have not talked to Alastair Duncan about this matter, so I do not know whether my mind is playing tricks on me. But to the best of my memory, that is the way I took that meeting. I'm not sure when -- it says "Kordic turned up." I'm quite sure that we drank toasts as well. And I also seem to remember, and my diary confirms that, that the ICRC were present, and I did not make such statements until they had departed. It was only after they had gone because I was conscious of trying to avoid being entangled or them associated with something that I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me switch to another occasion and then we'll come back to the 9th of May. In your book at page 310, you recounted a meeting with Dario Kordic in which Mr. Kordic had suggested that the Serbs had been responsible for Ahmici. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you find that an incredible explanation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. I just -- I remember laughing myself sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such an explanation to you for Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I would definitely agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such a statement to me, that the Serbs were responsible for that action, which, of course, goes to show, you know, that Kordic was not a soldier; otherwise, he would not have made such an outrageous statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that same day, demonstrating the kind of balance you had spoken of, you paid a visit on General Hadzihasanovic. Do you see that in the last page of your diary, for 9 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you note, on the 9th of May, that: "Apparently there are still some perhaps 300 plus HVO prisoners in Zenica which isn't too good and displeases Claire as the HVO have released all their prisoners in Vitez."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I remember that Claire was extremely angry that her part, which was working with the HVO, she had got all the people that were required to be released out, and I remember she was displeased because she felt the ICRC had not done their job in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask the registrar to please distribute Defence Exhibit 592. This is an article from Reuters dated April 24th, 1993, Vitez, headline "Croat Commander Promises Inquiry Into Family's Death." Why don't you take a moment to review this, paying particular attention to the person being reviewed and whether the name is correct? If the registrar could be pulling Exhibit 340 while we're discussing Exhibit D592, I would be appreciative. Does this article in part recount an interview with you, Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm confused by the article, Your Honour, but I suppose it must have been with me. Brian Watters was my second in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference at the beginning of paragraph 2 to, "Colonel Bob Waters, commander of British U.N. forces in Vitez," would you agree that that's actually a reference to you and not to Lieutenant-Colonel Watters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: He was a Major at the time. I'm not sure of which way to go, but I would suspect it was Colonel Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the third paragraph, and I'll read the prior paragraph so that it can be fully translated -- well, I'll start at the top: "A Croatian commander has acknowledged that the area where a family was brutally burned to death in a predominantly Muslim village was under his command, a British U.N. military spokesman said on Saturday. "Colonel Bob Waters, commander of British U.N. forces in Vitez in Central Bosnia, said that he had protested to the commander of Bosnian Croat forces in the region, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and demanded action against the perpetrators." Again, this is on the 24th -- the story is dated 24 April, 1993. "I asked Colonel Blaskic if the HVO (Croat militia) were responsible, and he said, 'It did happen in his area,' Waters said. 'I am clear he is absolutely horrified at what has taken place.'" Is that correct, Colonel, that on the 24th of April, 1993, you were clear -- it was clear in your mind that Colonel Blaskic was absolutely horrified at what had occurred Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that confirms what I said earlier, that I had the impression that he was upset by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word earlier used was "shocked," and I wanted to be more precise, and thank you for confirming this account. Now, on down the page, before we leave D592, there is a discussion of an investigative tribunal, and here your name is used with respect to the quotation: "Stewart said he wrote to Blaskic demanding action against those responsible for the killings and was told that a tribunal would be set up to investigate. 'But I said that for (the tribunal) to have any credence, the Muslims must also be represented,' Stewart said." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's entirely accurate. I'm not sure that we agreed that a tribunal be set up, I can't remember that, but I remember asking for it, as I earlier testified, and I already remember insisting that the Bosnian Muslim representation should be on that tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a meeting at which the HVO and the BH army was present at a high level to discuss the formation of a joint commission to investigate Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether, after you received Colonel Blaskic's letter of the 23rd of April, 1993, did you speak with (readcted) about possible ECMM assistance in an investigation, a joint multiparty investigation of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't recall it, but it's exactly what I would have done without the (redacted), because the ECMM, I felt, were more appropriate to investigate such a matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with Colonel Blaskic on the 24th of April, didn't he agree that something positive, in the nature of an investigation, did need to be done?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall. But I would hope that he did. I can't recall exactly -- well, I can't recall, is the answer, Your Honour. I would hope he would have said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you know about him, do you think it's likely that he would have wanted an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is likely that he would have wanted an investigation, but I don't know what happened, what orders he gave, because certainly nothing happened during my time in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'd like to have the last part reinterpreted. What was your question? Would you ask your question again, please? According to what you know about Colonel Blaskic, do you think that he would have or that he did? I'm asking the interpreter to clarify it for me. And the answer seems not to be the same to me. What is the answer to that? Would you give us your answer again, please, Colonel Stewart, whether he would have or whether he did?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did. I think he would have. But I never saw any evidence, Your Honour, of any action as a follow-up. As I say, Your Honour, this man, until this time, was someone I respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you said that. All right. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that what then happened was the U.N. Commission for Human Rights dispatched certain investigators to the area, and they, in fact, conducted an investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. They were there very quickly, Your Honour. I was surprised by the speed with which they were there, within a couple of days, as I recall. Their names were Thomas Osorio and Payam Akhavan, and Mr. Osorio spoke Croatian, Serbian, whatever you want to call it, fluently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they went to Zenica, or one of them, and interviewed persons who fled or victims; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they made an inspection at the scene?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct. They also asked me to investigate house number 7, and house number 7 was where we found further remains, as I recall dogs eating the bodies when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they the ones that, on or about the 4th of May, told you that, in their view, the civil government of the HVO in Vitez and Tihomir Blaskic were guilty of something?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: They probably are, but that was also my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they told you that they had gathered four names as suspects, possible perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with those individuals, Mr. Osorio and Mr. Akhavan, on the 4th of May, 1993, and was it agreed that that information, the four suspects, those names would not be shared with Colonel Blaskic or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly met with them. I don't know whether the date was accurate. I certainly checked with them that I could make public the names, to the appropriate authorities, and I discussed with them whether, in fact, we should make this publicly aware to everyone. I do not recall that we decided absolutely not to give the names to the HVO, but I think I probably said I would not give the names to the HVO, and my decision was probably that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I did that as well, because I wanted -- if they were suspicious, if people were suspicious, I didn't want them to disappear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at your diary, if you would, for May 4th, the carry over page, the bottom of the second paragraph. Do you see the line, "I agreed," and this is in the context of speaking to these gentlemen: "I agreed to raise the matter with Valentin and Blaskic without giving them names."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was discussed, and that was the agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's more accurate than what I've just said, but that's fundamentally the same gist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that because Colonel Blaskic, by the 4th of May, had become the target or a target of an investigation into who was responsible for the Ahmici massacre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely not. At the time, at that period, I was more concerned with actually who had done it on the ground. I wanted those people brought to justice as soon as possible. And the fact of the matter was, in my mind, and it's not in any diary, in my mind, I was not accusing Tihomir Blaskic of anything. Quite the reverse. At the time, I wanted him to help his cause, the HVO cause, by getting those responsible brought to justice, and if you will recall, in my evidence -- in that evidence, I repeatedly said, "This will go against the HVO if this is not investigated properly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why not give the names of the HVO members to Colonel Blaskic so he could have them arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Simply because I didn't want those people to disappear, and that probably was what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was your and the ECMM view that Colonel Blaskic could not be trusted with this information, so you wouldn't give it to him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's probably true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, would this be a convenient point to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, it would. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
